headline: Hiring a Framing Contractor for a Door Opening: What to Verify Before Work Begins
articleBody:
Cutting into an existing wall to frame a new doorway changes the structure of your home, and doing it right protects your finishes down the line. Before you bring in a contractor or finalize your plans, having complete clarity on the process saves both time and budget.

Overview
Door framing involves more than nailing two studs together. It requires understanding load paths, transferring weight down through king and jack studs, installing an appropriately sized header, and leaving the exact rough opening specified by the door manufacturer.

Key Benefits
A properly framed doorway ensures your door hangs plumb, latches smoothly, and prevents drywall cracking above the corners. Getting it right from day one also guarantees that finish casing sits flush without awkward shimming.

Process Breakdown
- What to Prepare Before You Start: Pick the exact door unit first. Standard rules often suggest adding two inches to slab width and two to two-and-a-half inches to slab height, but manufacturer specs govern. Check finished flooring thickness in advance so the threshold sits level.
- Structural Assessment: Determine if the wall carries floor or roof loads. Load-bearing walls require temporary shoring while old studs are removed and new headers are placed.
- Rough Framing: King studs, jack studs, header lumber, and cripple studs are measured and fastened. Diagonal measurements must match to confirm the frame is dead square.

Real Examples
When remodeling basements or updating main-floor layouts across Denver or Aurora, homeowners often want wider walk-throughs. If plumbing or wiring runs through the bay, framing must adapt safely around mechanicals.
